newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian retail sector seen needing boost.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian retail sector seen needing boost.

text.p: Australian Retailers Association chief executive Phil Naylor said on Thursday it would take more than an interest rate cut to boost the retail sector.

"Traditionally, a rate cut is beneficial to the retail industry in that it establishes more confidence in the community and also it provides more funds for retail sales, but I'm not so sure that that will necessarily happen on this occasion," Naylor told Australian Broadcasting Corp radio.
"I think there are some more fundamental things underlying the economy that are affecting retail sales."
Naylor said the retail sector was suffering as a result of continuing uncertainty in the economy and because of difficulties in passing on price increases to the consumer.

He said although the retailing sector had been through the worst of the downturn, he disagreed with Australian Treasurer Peter Costello's prediction that the country was about to enter a period of fast growth.
"I suspect that we may be still in tough times for the next six months or so, and then an interest rate cut, whilst welcome, probably won't have an immediate effect," he said.
"It may have a cumulative effect over the six months or so."
Naylor said the industry encouraged the Reserve Bank of Australia to consider dropping rates.

"We're not saying that won't be helpful, but I'm not certain that that will be the sole saviour for the retail industry," he said. "It's really a very competitive economy at the moment and retailers have to just readdress where they are and find what different things they can do to attract customers back."
Wednesday's inflation data, showing inflation was at its lowest level for two years, has prompted renewed speculation that the Reserve Bank will cut rates soon, possibly in November.
The market expects wages data for August, due out at 0130 GMT (11.30 a.m.) today, to provide further support to the argument for an interest rate cut.
Economists surveyed by Reuters expect wages to show a 1.0 percent rise in the three months to August, to be 3.7 percent higher over the year.
